projectTitle: dogmaOS — programming translation rhythm for soluble protein expression
tagline: Design where and for how long the ribosome should pause, then re-engineer the host tRNA pool to make that pause possible.
summary: XJTLU-China asked whether soluble yield of hard-to-express recombinant proteins in E. coli can be improved by deliberately programming *where* translation slows down, rather than by maximising expression. Their dry-lab system catmaOS (Codon-Aware Translation Modeling and Analysis Operating System) chains four models: structural co-translational folding priority (M1), evolutionary conserved slow-codon evidence (M2), a five-layer translation-kinetics and ribosome-traffic engine with constrained Pareto selection (M3-A to M3-E), and host tRNA-pool intervention design (M4). The framework picked a single synonymous G-CSF design (W1-S) out of six candidates and an engineered BL21-AlaPro chassis, both of which went to the bench; Four-Leaf Clover RT-qPCR then measured the actual tRNA knockdown and that number was fed back into M3-A as an updated host context. It won Best Model (Undergraduate) and Best Education (Undergraduate).

dry.frameworks: catmaOS is a four-model, five-layer multiscale pipeline and is unusually explicit about what each layer is and is not. M1 is a structural-bioinformatics scoring model: it builds a residue-level evidence table from PDB coordinates (G-CSF, PDB 1RHG chain B, UniProt P09919, RefSeq NM_000759.4), runs DSSP for secondary structure and relative solvent accessibility, solves a self-consistent native-contact occupancy model as chain length grows (Jacobs-Shakhnovich) to detect folding events at a 1 kBT free-energy-drop threshold with a 4 Angstrom contact cutoff, adds Kyte-Doolittle hydrophobic exposure, cysteine-neighbourhood scores, DSSP transition and beta-initiation tracks and an AGGRESCAN-style aggregation propensity, then fuses them with availability-aware weights into a 0-100 priority score and shifts it downstream by a 35-codon ribosome exit-tunnel offset (scanned 30-40 codons for sensitivity). M2 is a comparative-genomics model: MAFFT L-INS-i protein alignment projected back to codons with PAL2NAL, GtRNAdb/tRNAscan-SE high-confidence tRNA gene copy numbers per species, a frozen codon-anticodon wobble-penalty table, a tRNA-adaptation-style effective supply W_s(c) converted to within-species relative 'resistance', a top-25%-resistance slow-codon label, a strict same-amino-acid filter, and Henikoff position-based sequence weighting to produce a weighted slow-codon conservation score with an explicit effective-coverage track. M3 is the kinetic core: M3-A decomposes intrinsic codon dwell into decoding (inverse effective cognate/wobble supply with a near-cognate competition term, K_dec = 0.80, gamma_near = 0.50), peptidyl-transfer (proline/EF-P arrest context), basal translocation and ViennaRNA RNAplfold local-unpaired-probability RNA resistance, with four ablation configurations A0-A3 to attribute mechanism; M3-B feeds that rate vector into TWO independent ribosome-traffic backends — a deterministic Ribosome Flow Model with Extended Objects (RFMEO) steady state and a stochastic Gillespie kinetic Monte Carlo extended-object TASEP (5 replicates, SEM bands, warm-up discarded) — and cross-validates them with Pearson, Spearman, concordance and top-k hotspot overlap plus an alpha-beta boundary-sensitivity grid; M3-C maps traffic-safe dwell envelopes, exit-tunnel availability gates, relative contact-order folding demand, a finite-state productive-pathway propagator p_{L+1} = p_L exp(s Q_L dt_L) run over a 0.5/1/2 scale grid (direction called 'robust' only when the sign holds across scales), and a time-weighted unsatisfied-native-contact exposure proxy E_U = sum_L U(L) tau(L); M3-D closes a first-order steady-state mRNA balance M_ss = k_tx / (k_deg,eff + mu) with a scikit-learn mRNA-decay predictor trained on 5,486 curated E. coli half-life records (Chen 2015, Selinger 2003) split gene-grouped 3,883/765/838; M3-E generates synonymous candidates under reading-frame, GC, motif, restriction-site and homopolymer constraints and selects by constrained Pareto dominance over four frozen objectives (maximise terminal flux J, minimise ribosome load R, maximise productive-pathway C4, minimise exposure C5), with exact enumeration for small spaces and NSGA-II for large ones, scored for precision/recall against exact fronts. M4 extends design to the host: it maps target codons to BL21 tRNA genes, clusters and promoters with a weighted K-12-to-BL21 transfer score (S_map = 0.45 S_signature + 0.20 S_ordered + 0.15 S_count + 0.15 I_80 + 0.05 I_200), proposes copy-number reduction or 1-3 substitutions in a 29-bp promoter core against 15/30/50% weakening tiers, and ranks them with a three-model ML ensemble trained on 112,955 measured core promoters from the published MBRS L4 library (Zhou 2025), held out by -35/-10 motif pairs (67,978/7,680/37,297) achieving r = 0.677, MAE = 0.506 on log2(1+strength).
dry.dataviz: Eighteen numbered model figures that read as a single argument. Aligned multi-track profiles put six normalised structural feature tracks (F1-F6) above the availability-aware composite score so a reader can see which feature drove a peak; priority profiles are paired with an evidence-coverage track underneath so a high score with thin evidence cannot be misread as a finding. Figure 8 is a tunnel-length sensitivity heatmap (rows = assumed exit-tunnel length 30-40 codons, columns = codon position, fixed 0-100 teal scale, light-grey cells for genuinely unavailable data rather than zero) so the reader can watch high-priority bands migrate as an assumption changes. Figure 11 is a codon-level audit matrix (18 homolog rows x codons 110-121, green = slow in that species' tRNA context, white = comparable, grey = non-comparable). Figure 14 is a log2(candidate/WT) dwell heatmap restricted to edited positions only, with the x-axis explicitly flagged as non-continuous and the legend explaining that +1 means 2x. Figure 16 is a three-panel dot plot of WT-normalised flux, ribosome load and exposure on matched candidate rows, deliberately NOT collapsed into one score. KMC traces carry +/- SEM bands and separate unblocked residence from blocked waiting. Captions state the direction of preference and whether a quantity is measured or a relative model proxy.
dry.datascience: Two supervised models were trained from public measurement data and one from their own: an mRNA degradation proxy (D2) on 5,486 curated E. coli half-life records with gene/protein/CDS-grouped splits, a 29-bp promoter-strength ensemble on 112,955 measured core promoters held out by -35/-10 motif pairs (a genuinely out-of-distribution split, r = 0.677), and a codon-occupancy regression on 107,627 codon-level Ribo-seq observations across 125 genes with a documented 14-nt P-site offset, first/last 10 codons excluded, and gene-held-out evaluation (22,025 test observations). The team audits its own provenance in public: several dataset source fields are annotated 'unconfirmed', 'remains to be confirmed' or 'not an attributed published dataset size' rather than quietly cited. Model 4's proL promoter screen predicted 0.727 (native) vs 0.386/0.366/0.358 (P1-P3); the built strain BL21-AlaPro was then measured by Four-Leaf Clover RT-qPCR, showing rpoD-normalised mature tRNA falling from 63.98 to 23.42 (alaXW) and 6.828 to 2.254 (proL), and those measured numbers were returned to M3-A as a new effective-supply table for a full A-E rerun. The headline wet-lab readout: TolB-G-CSF model-designed sequence in the engineered host reached a mean soluble/insoluble ratio of 0.140 vs 0.075 for the commercial sequence in WT host (DnaK-normalised, n = 3 biological replicates, ~1.87-fold). Crucially the team also reports the negative result honestly — for PfCHT1 and leptin, insoluble bands weakened but no clear soluble enrichment appeared, and the results figure is literally titled 'Solubility Gains Remain Unclear'.
dry.software: catmaOS 4.02.06 ships as a downloadable Windows x64 source release with Setup.cmd/Start.cmd, a pinned requirements-lock.txt, a private .venv, a local browser workspace on 127.0.0.1:8767 (sequences never leave the user's machine), a 28-page PDF user manual, and four precomputed read-only interactive demos embedded in the wiki with JSON/CSV export. Every run emits a reproducibility bundle: request.json (typed input, label, source, parameters), result.json on a versioned schema 1.0.0 with input hash, module status and reproducibility record, curves.csv, metrics.csv, exact_candidates.csv, native/evidence-result.json and run.log, all zipped per run_id. The design rule stated on the page — 'missing values stay missing' and 'a completed run confirms the requested task finished; it does not imply every model was executed' — is the discipline most teams lack.
techniques: exit-tunnel coordinate mapping with sensitivity scan
stochastic Gillespie kinetic Monte Carlo TASEP with extended objects
machine-learning regression (promoter strength, mRNA decay, codon occupancy)

good.publicEngagement: Best Education winner (Undergraduate). The team built an explicit education framework rather than a list of events: a four-tier 'Lifelong Learning Pathway' (interest inspiration, knowledge building, interdisciplinary co-creation, professional impact) that replaces age-banding with depth of engagement, crossed with a four-stage activity structure (Reach, Construct, Dialogue, Extension) and Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences as the design lens for choosing an activity format. They reached over 2,000 people through 21 activities — workshops, exhibitions and the Learning Mall Premium online platform — and produced 18 reusable education toolkits, with the Extension stage deliberately designed so each activity leaves behind a game, handbook or toolkit rather than ending at the event.
good.ihp: A CARE framework distilled from stakeholder conversations: Create Accessibility, Accountable Storytelling, Real-world Alignment, Ethical Design. It originated in a question from Dr Lanlan Han about who actually benefits and how strong the evidence is. The interview timeline is structured as Problem / Design / Scope, and the team documents how it narrowed its own claim: starting from 'boost heterologous protein expression in E. coli', literature and interviews with Dr Antony Kam and industry expert Dr Xijun Piao (CATUG Biotechnology, Suzhou) pushed them to redefine success as soluble usable protein rather than total expression, and to state explicitly that dogmaOS is 'not positioned as a universal protein-production platform'. Mid-stage consultations with Dr Yongtao Zhu, Dr Chun Chan, Prof Sheng Yang (Shanghai Institutes for Biological Sciences, CAS), Prof Zhiliang Lu, Dr Avinash Pandreka (Oxford Suzhou Centre for Advanced Research), Dr Kozo Hamada and Prof Zhongmei Liu (Jiangnan University) convinced them that translation speed alone could not explain folding outcomes, which is what created Model 3 and Model 4.
good.realWorld: Target selection was driven by real demand: G-CSF, leptin, PfCHT1 and FGF2 were chosen with researchers and protein-production companies as proteins that are hard to express in E. coli and have clear research or clinical uses spanning public health, rare disease and basic research. The team maps the project to SDGs 3, 9, 12 and 17. Accessibility is the commercial thesis — rather than selling a service, catmaOS is released as free local software so academic labs and iGEM teams with only basic E. coli facilities can do upstream optimisation instead of paying for repeated trial-and-error. Safety is built in: non-pathogenic strains, BSL-1 practice, autoclaved waste, and FLP-FRT removal of the kanamycin cassette after lambda-Red genome editing.

images.caption: Figure 8: exit-tunnel sensitivity heatmap. Rows are assumed ribosome exit-tunnel lengths of 30-40 codons, columns are G-CSF codon positions, and the fixed 0-100 teal scale shows structural priority. Light-grey cells mark genuinely unavailable structural data rather than a score of zero, so the reader can watch high-priority bands migrate as a modelling assumption changes.

Figure 11: codon-level audit matrix for reference positions 110-121. Each row is a retained homolog; green marks codons called slow in that species' own tRNA context, white marks other comparable synonymous codons, grey retains non-comparable cells. Positions 115 and 121 were slow in all 18 homologs while 118 was slow in none.

Figure 12: the full 'how long to pause' panel, linking synonymous candidate generation to intrinsic dwell (M3-A), kinetic Monte Carlo ribosome traffic with SEM bands (M3-B), folding trajectories and contact exposure (M3-C), the mRNA decay proxy (M3-D) and the constrained objective screen (M3-E) in which four of six candidates pass the flux and ribosome-burden gates.

Figure 16: throughput, ribosome load and exposure trade-offs for wild type plus six synonymous candidates, shown as three WT-normalised panels on matched rows and deliberately not collapsed into a single score. W1-F had flux 0.781 and load 1.079, failing the flux >= 0.95 constraint; W1-S passed on all four objectives and went to the bench.

gemsTakeaway: Pair every model score with an explicit evidence-coverage track and run a sensitivity scan over your least-defensible assumption (here, exit-tunnel length), so a figure shows not just the answer but how much of it is real data; and keep competing objectives as separate aligned panels rather than summing them into one invented score. Both are achievable with matplotlib by a motivated 16-year-old and immediately make a model honest.
